maths_eduqas_h.2.2.summary: Mastering scale factors, scale diagrams, and maps requires a seamless fluency in converting between ratio representations and real-world dimensions. Top-tier Grade 9 responses depend on recognising the multiplicative link between lengths, as well as handling area and volume scaling correctly when given linear multipliers. Precision with units, map scales, and bearings on scale drawings are essential core skills for both non-calculator and calculator papers.

core.p: A scale factor is a multiplier that describes how much a figure or dimension is enlarged or reduced. When dealing with linear scale factors, every corresponding length is multiplied by the exact same value.
bullets: A scale factor greater than 1 represents an enlargement.
A scale factor between 0 and 1 represents a reduction.
A scale factor of 1 means the shape remains congruent.
Corresponding lengths scale linearly, meaning if scale factor is k, length becomes k times original.

callouts.p: The ratio of any two corresponding lengths in two similar geometric figures.
Never apply a linear scale factor directly to areas or volumes without squaring or cubing it first.

core.p: Maps represent large geographical areas on a small sheet of paper by using a fixed ratio. To interpret a map scale correctly, both sides of the ratio must be in the exact same unit of measurement.
bullets: A map scale of 1:50000 means 1 cm on the map represents 50000 cm in real life.
Always convert centimetres to metres or kilometres to make real-life distances meaningful.
100 cm = 1 m, and 100000 cm = 1 km.
Map ratios are dimensionless, meaning units cancel out when written purely as a ratio.

callouts.p: Always convert map measurements into the same physical units before attempting any calculation.

core.p: Scale diagrams require precise measurements using a ruler and protractor. Every line segment must be drawn to the exact specified proportion to earn full marks in examination conditions.
bullets: Read the given scale carefully, such as '1 cm represents 2 metres'.
Use a sharp pencil and a clean plastic ruler for accuracy.
Check that right angles are constructed accurately using set squares or protractors.
Label all vertices and key dimensions clearly on the final diagram.

callouts.p: Examiners generally allow a tolerance of +/- 2 mm for plotted lengths and +/- 2 degrees for angles.

core.p: Many maps and architectural plans use a visual scale bar instead of a written ratio. A scale bar remains accurate even if the map or diagram is photocopied or resized digitally.
bullets: Measure the physical length of the scale bar using your ruler.
Set up an equivalence equation between measured cm and real-world units.
Measure the distance required on the diagram and multiply by the scale factor derived from the bar.
Avoid relying on printed numbers if the page has been scaled; always measure the bar itself.

callouts.p: Scale bars resize proportionally with the image, making them immune to digital resizing errors.

core.p: When a two-dimensional shape is enlarged by a linear scale factor k, its area does not scale by k. Because area depends on two dimensions (length and width), the area scale factor is k squared.
bullets: If linear scale factor is k, then Area Scale Factor = k squared.
If a shape is enlarged by scale factor 3, its area increases by a factor of 3 squared = 9.
To find the real area, multiply the scale diagram area by k squared.
To find the real linear dimension from an area ratio, take the square root of the area scale factor.

callouts.p: Ratio of areas of similar figures = (Linear Scale Factor)^2.

core.p: Three-dimensional similar shapes scale in volume according to the cube of the linear scale factor. Length, width, and height all scale by k, meaning volume scales by k cubed.
bullets: If linear scale factor is k, then Volume Scale Factor = k cubed.
If a solid is enlarged by scale factor 2, its volume increases by 2 cubed = 8 times.
To find the real volume, multiply the model volume by k cubed.
To find the linear scale factor from volumes, calculate the cube root of the volume ratio.

callouts.p: A common Grade 8/9 error is multiplying volume by 3 instead of cubing the linear scale factor.

core.p: Navigation problems frequently combine scale diagrams with three-figure bearings. A bearing is measured clockwise from North and must always be written using exactly three digits.
bullets: Always draw a faint North line at every point where a bearing is measured.
Measure angles clockwise from the North line using a protractor.
Combine scale length conversion with accurate angle plotting to locate positions.
Use alternate interior angles (Z-angles) on parallel North lines for back-bearings.

callouts.p: Draw North lines lightly in pencil at every turning point to prevent angular misreadings.

core.h: Converting Units of Area and Volume in Scaling
core.p: When dealing with scaled units, changing units before applying the scale factor is much safer than converting squared or cubed units afterwards.
bullets: 1 m = 100 cm, so 1 square metre = 100 cm x 100 cm = 10,000 square cm.
1 m = 100 cm, so 1 cubic metre = 100 cm x 100 cm x 100 cm = 1,000,000 cubic cm.
Convert linear dimensions first, then calculate area or volume.
Always check whether the question asks for cm squared or m squared.

callouts.p: Square the conversion factor for area; cube the conversion factor for volume.

core.p: Professional blueprints use standard ratios such as 1:50 or 1:100. Interpreting these requires translating floor plans into actual room dimensions and calculating total materials required.
bullets: Measure the length of a room on the blueprint in centimetres.
Multiply by the scale factor denominator to find the real-life measurement in centimetres.
Convert centimetres into metres for practical building dimensions.
Calculate real floor areas using area scale factors or by converting dimensions before multiplying.

callouts.p: Convert the map scale into a direct multiplier (e.g. 1 cm = 0.5 m) to speed up calculations.

core.p: Exam questions frequently provide the real-life dimension and ask you to find the measurement on a map or scale model. This requires dividing by the scale factor rather than multiplying.
bullets: Identify the scale ratio in the form 1 : n.
To go from real life to map/model, divide the real measurement by n.
Ensure both quantities are in the exact same unit before dividing.
Check that your final answer on the map is smaller when reducing to scale.

callouts.p: Do not multiply real-life values by the scale factor when trying to find map lengths; always divide.

core.p: Higher tier papers combine scale factors with compound measures such as density, speed, and pressure, requiring multi-step logical deductions.
bullets: If a scale model is made of the same material as the real object, its volume scales by k cubed.
Mass = Density x Volume. Since density is constant, mass scales by the exact same factor as volume (k cubed).
Check whether surface area scaling or volume scaling is required for pressure calculations (Pressure = Force / Area).
Set up clear proportional equations for each compound component.

callouts.p: Mass is directly proportional to volume for uniform material, so mass scales by k cubed.

analogy.p: Imagine building an OO-gauge model railway layout where the scale is 1:76. Every single dimension of a real locomotive is divided by 76 so it fits on your table. However, if you want to know how much heavier the real train is, you cannot just multiply by 76; because the train has length, width, and height, the real train's volume and mass are 76 cubed times heavier than the model. The analogy breaks down because real materials cannot always be scaled down in thickness while maintaining structural integrity (the square-cube law in biology and engineering).

terms.d: The ratio by which any length of a geometric figure is enlarged or reduced.
Figures that have the same shape, equal corresponding angles, and sides in constant proportion.
The ratio of map distance to corresponding real-world ground distance.
A scale expressed as a ratio without units, such as 1:25000.
A graphic line divided into units representing real-world distances on a map.
The multiplier k applied to 1D lengths between similar figures.
The multiplier k squared applied to 2D areas between similar figures.
The multiplier k cubed applied to 3D volumes between similar figures.
A direction measured clockwise as a three-digit angle from North.
An architectural or engineering scale drawing used for construction.
Identical in shape and size.
A ratio where both quantities share identical units and cancel out.

mistakes.w: Multiplying area by the linear scale factor k instead of k squared.
mistakes.r: Area scale factor is always the square of the linear scale factor (k^2).

mistakes.w: Forgetting to convert units when calculating map distances (e.g. mixing cm and km directly).
mistakes.r: Always convert both quantities into the exact same unit before setting up equations.

mistakes.w: Multiplying volume by 3 instead of cubing the linear scale factor.
mistakes.r: Volume scale factor is the cube of the linear scale factor (k^3).

mistakes.w: Multiplying instead of dividing when working backwards from real life to a map length.
mistakes.r: Divide real-life dimensions by the scale factor denominator to find the map length.

mistakes.w: Writing a bearing with fewer than three digits, such as 65 degrees instead of 065 degrees.
mistakes.r: All bearings must be written as a three-digit number.

mistakes.w: Measuring bearings anti-clockwise from North.
mistakes.r: Bearings are strictly measured in a clockwise direction from the North line.

mistakes.w: Assuming density changes when scaling a solid object.
mistakes.r: Density remains constant for uniform materials; mass scales proportionally with volume.

exam.q: On a map with a scale of 1:25000, the distance between two towns is 6 cm. Calculate the real-life distance in kilometres.
exam.tip: Always remember there are 100,000 cm in 1 km.

exam.q: Two solid metal spheres are mathematically similar. The smaller sphere has a radius of 3 cm and the larger sphere has a radius of 9 cm. Find the volume scale factor.
exam.tip: Find the linear scale factor first, then cube it for volume.

exam.q: A model of a bridge is built to a scale of 1:200. The surface area of the model is 450 cm^2. Calculate the surface area of the real bridge in square metres.
model: Convert to m^2 by dividing by 10000
exam.tip: Convert cm^2 to m^2 by dividing by 10,000 at the end.

exam.q: A map has a scale bar where 2 cm represents 5 km. Express this scale in the form 1 : n.
exam.tip: Both sides of the ratio must represent the exact same unit (cm).

exam.q: The volume of a child's toy car is 120 cm^3. The real car has a volume of 15 m^3. Find the linear scale factor of the model.
model: Convert real volume to cm^3: 15 m^3 = 15,000,000 cm^3
Linear scale factor = cube root of 125,000
exam.tip: Ensure both volumes are in the same units before finding the ratio.

exam.q: Ship A sails on a bearing of 070 degrees from port P for 8 cm on a scale drawing where 1 cm represents 10 km. Find the distance from port P in km.
model: Bearing 070 degrees is used for direction, distance is purely 80 km
exam.tip: Separate directional information (bearing) from magnitude (distance).

exam.q: Two similar containers have heights of 12 cm and 18 cm. The smaller container holds 400 ml of water. Work out the capacity of the larger container.
exam.tip: Fractional linear scale factors cube cleanly using decimals or improper fractions.

exam.q: A rectangular park has an area of 0.12 km^2. On a plan, the area of the park is 30 cm^2. Find the map scale in the form 1 : n.
model: Linear scale factor = square root of 40,000,000
exam.tip: Be extremely careful with area unit conversions when squaring and rooting.

exam.q: A statue has a mass of 4.5 tonnes. A scale model of the statue is made from the same bronze material with a linear scale factor of 1:10. Find the mass of the model in kilograms.
model: Mass scales by the same factor as volume
exam.tip: Mass is proportional to volume when material density is uniform.

worked.q: A garden is represented on a plan with a scale of 1:200. On the plan, the rectangular lawn measures 6 cm by 4.5 cm. (a) Calculate the actual dimensions of the lawn in metres. (b) Calculate the actual area of the lawn in square metres.
steps: For part (a), multiply each plan dimension by 200 to get actual cm: Length = 6 x 200 = 1200 cm; Width = 4.5 x 200 = 900 cm.
Convert actual cm to metres by dividing by 100: Actual length = 12 m; Actual width = 9 m.
For part (b), calculate actual area directly: Area = 12 m x 9 m = 108 m^2.
Alternatively, use area scale factor: Plan area = 6 x 4.5 = 27 cm^2. Area scale factor = 200^2 = 40,000. Real area = 27 x 40,000 = 1,080,000 cm^2. Convert to m^2 by dividing by 10,000 to get 108 m^2.

worked.q: Two similar jugs, A and B, have base diameters of 8 cm and 12 cm respectively. Jug A has a height of 15 cm and holds 500 ml of juice. (a) Find the height of Jug B. (b) Find the capacity of Jug B in millilitres.
steps: Find the linear scale factor k from the given diameters: k = 12 / 8 = 1.5.
For part (a), multiply Jug A's height by the linear scale factor: Height of Jug B = 15 x 1.5 = 22.5 cm.
For part (b), calculate the volume scale factor by cubing the linear scale factor: Volume SF = 1.5 cubed = 3.375.
Multiply Jug A's capacity by the volume scale factor: Capacity of Jug B = 500 x 3.375 = 1687.5 ml.

maths_eduqas_h.2.8.summary: Mastering the connections between ratios, fractions, and linear functions is a crucial Grade 9 skill for the Eduqas GCSE Higher tier. This topic bridges the gap between arithmetic sharing and coordinate geometry, allowing you to represent ratios as coordinate pairs, algebraic lines, and proportional fractions. By understanding how parts of a ratio translate into fractional components of a whole and how those fractions form straight-line graphs, you unlock advanced problem-solving techniques for complex algebraic and geometric contexts.

core.p: Converting between ratios and fractions is the fundamental building block for higher-level proportional reasoning. When a quantity is split into a ratio a : b, the total number of parts is a + b. Each part can then be expressed as a fraction of the whole. This allows you to transition smoothly from comparing parts of a set to evaluating a part relative to the entire system.
bullets: For a ratio $a : b$, the total number of parts is $a + b$.
The first quantity represents the fraction $\frac{a}{a+b}$ of the total.
The second quantity represents the fraction $\frac{b}{a+b}$ of the total.
Fractions can be converted back to ratios by looking at the numerators of parts that share the same denominator.

callouts.p: If quantity $x$ and quantity $y$ are in the ratio $a : b$, then $x = \frac{a}{a+b} \times \text{Total}$ and $y = \frac{b}{a+b} \times \text{Total}.
Always sum the ratio parts first. Forgetting to add them together is the single most common error when converting ratios to fractions.

core.p: Going in reverse requires expressing given fractional amounts as a ratio in its simplest form. If you know that quantity P is $\frac{3}{7}$ of a total and quantity Q is $\frac{4}{7}$, the ratio P : Q is simply $3 : 4$. When fractions have different denominators, you must find a common denominator to compare them directly as a ratio.
bullets: If $A = \frac{2}{5}T$ and $B = \frac{3}{5}T$, then $A : B = 2 : 3$.
To compare fractional parts of different wholes, convert them to equivalent fractions with a common denominator.
Simplify integer ratios by dividing by the highest common factor (HCF).
Fractional ratios like $\frac{1}{2} : \frac{1}{3}$ are simplified by multiplying by the lowest common multiple (LCM) of denominators.

callouts.p: You cannot write a direct ratio of two quantities if they are fractions of different totals, unless you first scale them to the same absolute value.

core.p: Ratios can be treated as operators or multipliers that scale one quantity to find another. If $x : y = 4 : 7$, then $y = \frac{7}{4}x$ and $x = \frac{4}{7}y$. Viewing ratios as multiplicative operators connects directly to linear scaling and function notation.
bullets: The ratio $x : y = a : b$ can be written as the equation $y = \frac{b}{a}x$.
The multiplier $\frac{b}{a}$ acts as the scale factor transforming $x$ into $y$.
Inverse relationships are found by inverting the ratio fraction: if $y = \frac{b}{a}x$, then $x = \frac{a}{b}y$.
Multipliers can be decimals, fractions, or surds in higher-tier questions.

callouts.p: The multiplier $\frac{b}{a}$ is the constant of proportionality, often denoted as $k$, giving the direct proportion equation $y = kx.

core.p: A linear function is of the form $y = mx + c$. When two variables are in a constant ratio $x : y = a : b$, they form a direct proportion linear function passing through the origin, where the y-intercept $c = 0$ and the gradient $m = \frac{b}{a}$ (or $\frac{a}{b}$ depending on which variable is dependent).
bullets: The statement 'y is in a constant ratio to x' means $y = kx$ where $k$ is a constant.
The graph of a ratio relationship is a straight line through the origin $(0,0)$.
The gradient of the line represents the ratio value expressed as a unit rate.
Shifting the ratio relationship by a constant amount creates a linear function of the form $y = mx + c$ where $c \neq 0$.

callouts.p: A function representing a direct ratio has the form $f(x) = mx$ where $m > 0$.

core.p: Any point $(x, y)$ lying on a line representing a ratio $a : b$ satisfies the condition that $x : y$ simplifies to $a : b$. In exam questions, you may be given coordinates and asked whether they satisfy a given ratio, or to find missing coordinates using proportional triangles under the line.
bullets: If point $(X, Y)$ lies on $y = \frac{b}{a}x$, then $X : Y = a : b$.
Similar right-angled triangles formed under the line confirm the constancy of the ratio.
Scaling coordinates by a factor $k$ moves along the line while preserving the ratio.
Algebraic coordinates like $(t, kt)$ always maintain the ratio $1 : k$.

callouts.p: Draw a right-angled triangle under the line with horizontal step $a$ and vertical rise $b$ to instantly read off the ratio.

core.p: Higher-tier Eduqas papers often link ratio statements directly to linear simultaneous equations. Translating a sentence like "the ratio of $x$ to $y$ is $2:3$, and their sum is $40$" into algebraic equations allows you to solve for both variables efficiently.
bullets: Translate ratio statements into algebraic equations: $x : y = a : b$ becomes $\frac{x}{y} = \frac{a}{b}$ or $bx = ay$.
Combine with linear constraint equations (e.g., $x + y = k$) to form a solvable system.
Use substitution: express one variable in terms of the other using the ratio multiplier, then substitute into the constraint equation.
Verify solutions by checking that the resulting values simplify back to the original ratio.

callouts.p: The ratio equation $\frac{x}{y} = \frac{a}{b}$ can be rewritten without fractions using cross-multiplication: $bx = ay$.

core.p: Connecting ratios to linear functions enables the coordinate geometry technique of dividing a line segment in a given ratio $m : n$. By examining the horizontal and vertical distances between two points, you can calculate the exact coordinates of the dividing point using linear fractional increments.
bullets: To divide line segment AB from $(x_1, y_1)$ to $(x_2, y_2)$ in the ratio $m : n$:
The x-coordinate is $x_1 + \frac{m}{m+n}(x_2 - x_1)$.
The y-coordinate is $y_1 + \frac{m}{m+n}(y_2 - y_1)$.
This is a direct application of fractional linear interpolation between two points.

callouts.p: Point dividing $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$ in ratio $m:n$ is $\left( \frac{nx_1 + mx_2}{m+n}, \frac{ny_1 + my_2}{m+n} \right)$.

core.h: Direct Proportion and Linear Graphs ($y = kx$)
core.p: Direct proportion is a specific type of linear function where the graph is a straight line passing through the origin. The ratio between the two variables remains constant everywhere on the line. Understanding how to extract the ratio from the gradient is essential for top grades.
bullets: Equation format: $y = kx$, where $k$ is the constant of proportionality.
The ratio $y : x$ is always equal to $k : 1$.
The gradient of the line is equal to $k$.
Any point $(x, y)$ on the graph gives the ratio $x : y = 1 : k$ or $y : x = k : 1$.

callouts.p: If a straight line does not pass through $(0,5)$, the variables are NOT in direct proportion, even though the relationship is linear ($y = mx + c$). Ratios require $c = 0$.

core.h: Inverse Proportion and Hyperbolic Functions ($xy = k$)
core.p: While direct proportion relates to linear functions, inverse proportion relates to non-linear hyperbolic functions. If two variables are inversely proportional, their product is constant ($xy = k$). This means that as one variable increases, the other decreases in a non-linear fashion.
bullets: Equation format: $y = \frac{k}{x}$ or $xy = k$.
Can be viewed through reciprocal ratios: as $x$ scales by factor $n$, $y$ scales by factor $\frac{1}{n}$.
The graph is a rectangular hyperbola in the first and third quadrants.
Inverse proportion is tested on Higher tier papers to contrast with direct linear ratio functions.

callouts.p: In inverse proportion, the product of corresponding values is always constant: $x_1 y_1 = x_2 y_2 = k$.

core.p: Sometimes, exam questions require you to rearrange formulae where variables are defined by a ratio. For example, if the base and height of a triangle are in the ratio $3 : 4$, you can substitute $b = 3t$ and $h = 4t$ into the area formula to find an expression in terms of a single variable $t$.
bullets: Substitute ratio variables using a common scaling variable $t$.
For ratio $p : q : r$, let the quantities be $pt$, $qt$, and $rt$.
Substitute these expressions into geometric or algebraic formulae (Area, Volume, Perimeter).
Solve for $t$ and then back-substitute to find the individual actual lengths or quantities.

callouts.p: Introducing a dummy variable $t$ is the most robust way to handle multi-part ratio algebraic substitutions without making fraction errors.

core.p: Grade 9 questions often combine ratio, fractions, and linear functions in context. You might be given a cost function or a profit margin split in a ratio that changes dynamically with production volume $x$. Mastery requires setting up algebraic expressions for each part and equating them to given linear constraints.
bullets: Break down complex word problems into distinct linear expressions for each ratio part.
Form an equation representing the total sum or difference.
Solve for the scaling factor or variable.
Interpret your algebraic solution back into ratio and fractional terms as required by the final question prompt.

callouts.p: If the question asks for a fraction, do not leave your answer as a ratio. Always convert your final algebraic result into the exact format requested.

core.p: Higher tier Eduqas papers may express ratios using function notation. For instance, given a function $f(x)$, you may be told that $f(x) : x = 3 : 2$. This requires setting up the algebraic equation $\frac{f(x)}{x} = \frac{3}{2}$ and solving for the function itself, linking core algebra with ratio principles.
bullets: Translate $f(x) : g(x) = a : b$ into the algebraic fraction $\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{a}{b}$.
Use cross-multiplication to find the functional relationship.
Evaluate the function at specific values of $x$ to find numerical ratio outputs.
Combine with composite and inverse functions in extension problems.

callouts.p: $f(x) : x = a : b \iff b f(x) = a x$ for all valid $x$.

analogy.p: Imagine making cordial squash: a recipe calls for juice and water in the ratio 1 : 4. This means juice is 1/5 of the total drink, and water is 4/5. If you plot the amount of juice ($x$) against water ($y$), you get a straight line $y = 4x$ passing through the origin with a gradient of 4. Where this analogy breaks down is that cordial mixing has physical capacity limits, whereas mathematical linear functions extend infinitely in both directions.

terms.d: A quantitative relation between two or more amounts showing the relative sizes of values.
A numerical quantity that is not a whole number, representing a part of a whole divided into equal parts.
A function whose graph is a straight line, typically written in the form $y = mx + c$.
A relationship between two quantities where the ratio of their values is constant ($y = kx$).
A relationship where an increase in one quantity results in a proportional decrease in the other ($xy = k$).
The constant multiplier $k$ that relates proportional quantities ($y = kx$).
A measure of the steepness of a line, calculated as vertical change divided by horizontal change.
The point where a graph crosses the y-axis, representing the value of $y$ when $x = 0$.
A fraction used to scale a quantity up or down in proportional calculations.
A technique to solve equation fractions by multiplying the numerator of one side by the denominator of the other.
Splitting a line segment into a given ratio using coordinate geometry fractions.
A method of writing algebraic rules using $f(x)$ to represent the output for input $x$.
A symbol, usually a letter, representing an unknown number in an expression or equation.
The state of being corresponding in size, degree, or intensity to something else.

mistakes.w: Writing the ratio $3 : 5$ as the fraction $\frac{3}{5}$ when referring to a part-to-part comparison
mistakes.r: Part-to-part ratios must use the sum of parts as the denominator for fractions of the whole: $\frac{3}{8}$ and $\frac{5}{8}$.

mistakes.w: Stating that $y = 2x + 3$ shows direct proportion because it involves multiplication
mistakes.r: Direct proportion requires a straight line passing through the origin ($c = 0$). Here, the y-intercept is 3.

mistakes.w: Inverting the fraction when converting a ratio $a : b$ into a linear function $y = mx$
mistakes.r: For ratio $x : y = a : b$, the function is $y = \frac{b}{a}x$, not $\frac{a}{b}x$.

mistakes.w: Dividing a quantity by the difference of ratio parts instead of their sum
mistakes.r: Always add the ratio parts together to find the total number of fractional parts ($a + b$).

mistakes.w: Assuming inverse proportion means negative gradient on a straight line
mistakes.r: Inverse proportion is represented by a curved rectangular hyperbola ($xy = k$), not a straight line.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to include the scaling variable $t$ when substituting a ratio into an algebraic formula
mistakes.r: Use $3t$ and $4t$ instead of just $3$ and $4$ when side lengths are unknown.

mistakes.w: Mixing up dependent and independent variables on coordinate ratio graphs
mistakes.r: The first term in a ratio $x : y$ corresponds to the horizontal axis ($x$), and the second to the vertical axis ($y$).

exam.q: The ratio of red beads to blue beads in a bag is $3 : 5$. What fraction of the total beads are blue?
exam.tip: Always calculate the total number of parts by adding the ratio numbers together first.

exam.q: Express the linear function $y = \frac{3}{4}x$ as a ratio of $x : y$ in its simplest integer form.
exam.tip: Pay careful attention to whether the question asks for x : y or y : x.

exam.q: A line represents the ratio $x : y = 2 : 7$. Write down the equation of the linear function representing $y$ in terms of $x$.
exam.tip: The vertical variable $y$ is the numerator when finding $y$ in terms of $x$.

exam.q: The ratio of boys to girls in a club is $4 : 3$. There are 84 members in total. Use fractions to find the number of girls.
exam.tip: Convert the ratio to a fraction of the total before multiplying by the overall quantity.

exam.q: Point P divides the line segment from $(-2, 1)$ to $(8, 11)$ in the ratio $2 : 3$. Find the coordinates of P.
exam.tip: Use the fractional increment formula for internal division of coordinates.

exam.q: Two variables, $p$ and $q$, are in the ratio $p : q = 5 : 2$. If $p + q = 49$, find the value of $p$ using fractional multipliers.
exam.tip: Fractional multipliers streamline the calculation compared to finding the value of a single share.

exam.q: A straight-line graph passes through the origin and the point $(4, 10)$. Write the equation of the line representing this proportional ratio.
exam.tip: Since it passes through the origin, use y = kx where k is the y-coordinate divided by the x-coordinate.

exam.q: The ratio of two numbers is $3 : 7$. When 12 is added to each, the ratio becomes $5 : 9$. Find the original numbers.
exam.tip: Use algebraic multipliers ($3x$ and $7x$) and set up a fractional equation.

exam.q: State whether the linear function $3x - 4y = 0$ represents a direct ratio between $x$ and $y$. Give a reason.
model: It can be rearranged to y = (3/4)x, which passes through the origin with no constant term
exam.tip: Check if the equation simplifies to y = kx with zero intercept.

exam.q: The function $f(x)$ is such that $f(x) : x = 7 : 3$. Find $f(6)$.
exam.tip: Convert the functional ratio into an algebraic equation before substituting the value.

worked.q: The ratio of water to flour in a dough mixture is $3 : 5$ by weight. If the total weight of the dough is 1.6 kg, use fractions to find the weight of the flour in grams.
steps: Step 1: Find the total number of parts in the ratio. Total parts = 3 + 5 = 8 parts.
Step 2: Express the weight of flour as a fraction of the total dough. Flour fraction = 5/8.
Step 3: Calculate the weight of flour in kg by multiplying the fraction by the total weight. Flour weight = (5/8) x 1.6 kg = 1.0 kg.
Step 4: Convert the result into grams as requested by the question. 1.0 kg = 1000 grams.

worked.q: A straight line graph represents the ratio $y : x = 4 : 3$. (a) Write the equation of the line in the form $y = mx$. (b) Determine whether the point $(9, 11)$ lies on this line.
steps: Step 1: Translate the ratio $y : x = 4 : 3$ into a linear function. Since $y$ is the vertical axis and $x$ is the horizontal axis, $\frac{y}{x} = \frac{4}{3}$, giving $y = \frac{4}{3}x$.
Step 2: Test point $(9, 11)$ by substituting $x = 9$ into the equation. $y = \frac{4}{3}(9) = 12$.
Step 3: Compare the calculated $y$-value ($12$) with the given $y$-coordinate ($11$). Since $12 \neq 11$, the point does not lie on the line.
worked.ans: (a) y = (4/3)x (b) No, because when x = 9, y = 12, not 11.

maths_eduqas_h.2.3.summary: Mastering the expression of one quantity as a fraction of another is an essential foundational skill for the Eduqas Higher Tier GCSE, where fractions frequently exceed 1. This topic requires setting up clear fractional relationships where the reference quantity (the 'whole' or the 'out of') is always placed in the denominator. Students must be fully confident in simplifying improper fractions, converting between mixed numbers and fractions, and manipulating algebraic expressions where quantities are represented symbolically rather than numerically.

core.p: To express quantity A as a fraction of quantity B, quantity A forms the numerator and quantity B forms the denominator. This represents the division A divided by B, establishing a direct part-to-whole relationship.
bullets: The reference quantity always forms the denominator.
Both quantities must be expressed in the exact same unit before forming the fraction.
The resulting fraction can be less than 1, equal to 1, or greater than 1.

callouts.p: An expression of the form A/B where A represents the part being considered and B represents the entire reference whole.
Always check the phrasing: 'express X as a fraction of Y' means X/Y, not Y/X.

fig.cap: Visualising quantity comparison where the numerator is smaller than the denominator, resulting in a fraction less than 1.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="20" y="20" width="360" height="200" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#cbd5e1" rx="8"/><rect x="40" y="60" width="320" height="50" fill="#e2e8f0" rx="4"/><rect x="40" y="60" width="200" height="50" fill="#3b82f6" rx="4"/><text x="200" y="92" fill="#ffffff" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">Part A = 4 (Numerator)</text><text x="40" y="145" fill="#1e293b" font-size="13">Whole B = 6 (Denominator)</text><text x="200" y="180" fill="#1e293b" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">Fraction = 4 / 6 = 2 / 3</text></svg>

core.p: When the quantity being compared is strictly smaller than the reference quantity, the resulting fraction is a proper fraction lying between 0 and 1. The numerator is smaller than the denominator.
bullets: Occurs when Numerator < Denominator.
Represents a genuine subset of a whole.
Must be fully simplified by dividing both numerator and denominator by their highest common factor (HCF).

callouts.p: Always check prime factorisations or use your calculator's fraction button to reduce proper fractions instantly.

core.h: 3. Fractions Greater Than 1 (Improper and Mixed Fractions)
core.p: In many Higher Tier exam contexts, the quantity being compared is larger than the reference quantity. This yields an improper fraction (top-heavy fraction) where the numerator exceeds the denominator, or equivalently a mixed number.
bullets: Occurs when Numerator > Denominator.
Represents more than one complete whole.
Can be written as an improper fraction (e.g., 7/4) or a mixed number (e.g., 1 and 3/4).

callouts.p: Unless the question explicitly asks for a mixed number, leaving your answer as an improper fraction (top-heavy) is fully accepted and preferred in algebraic work.

core.p: A frequent examiner trap is presenting the two quantities in different units. You must convert both quantities into the exact same unit before forming the fraction.
bullets: Convert larger units to smaller units to avoid decimals where possible (e.g., metres to centimetres, kilograms to grams, hours to minutes).
Check currency, mass, length, volume, and time units carefully.
Once units match, drop the unit labels entirely from the fraction.

callouts.p: Never write 40 cm as a fraction of 2 m as 40/2. Convert 2 m to 200 cm first, giving 40/200.

core.p: Time and money do not use base-10 systems, making them prime territory for fraction comparison errors. Minutes must be converted to fractions of an hour or kept strictly as minutes.
bullets: To express 45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours, convert 2 hours to 120 minutes.
Form the fraction: 45 / 120 = 3 / 8.
For money, convert pounds to pence if dealing with mixed decimal values, or keep as pounds with decimals.

callouts.p: Remember there are 60 minutes in an hour. Never write 0.45 hours when you mean 45 minutes.

core.p: Higher tier papers test your ability to express algebraic terms as fractions of other algebraic terms. The rules remain identical: the target quantity goes on top, the reference quantity goes on the bottom.
bullets: Express 3x as a fraction of 5y: write 3x / 5y.
Express 2(a + b) as a fraction of 4a: write 2(a + b) / 4a, then simplify by cancelling common factors.
Cancel algebraic common factors across numerator and denominator just like numerical HCFs.

callouts.p: Factorise expressions fully before attempting to cancel terms in fractions.

core.p: Exam questions often combine ratios with fractions. Understanding that a ratio part-to-whole relationship can be immediately rewritten as a fraction is vital for speed and accuracy.
bullets: If the ratio of red to blue counters is 3 : 5, the total parts equal 3 + 5 = 8.
Red counters are 3/8 of the total; blue counters are 5/8 of the total.
Red counters as a fraction of blue counters is 3/5.

callouts.p: Part-to-part compares subgroups (A/B); part-to-whole compares a subgroup to the grand total (A/(A+B)).

fig.cap: Distinction between part-to-part fractions and part-to-whole fractions derived from ratio components.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="20" y="20" width="360" height="200" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#cbd5e1" rx="8"/><rect x="40" y="50" width="120" height="40" fill="#ef4444" rx="4"/><rect x="170" y="50" width="180" height="40" fill="#3b82f6" rx="4"/><text x="100" y="75" fill="#ffffff" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">A = 3 parts</text><text x="260" y="75" fill="#ffffff" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">B = 4.5 parts</text><text x="40" y="130" fill="#1e293b" font-size="13">Part-to-part: A as fraction of B = 3 / 4.5 = 2 / 3</text><text x="40" y="165" fill="#1e293b" font-size="13">Part-to-whole: A as fraction of Total (7.5) = 3 / 7.5 = 2 / 5</text></svg>

core.h: 8. Percentage to Fraction Equivalents Greater Than 1
core.p: Fractions greater than 1 correspond directly to percentages greater than 100%. Converting between these representations is a common synoptic skill.
bullets: 125% written as a fraction is 125 / 100 = 5 / 4 = 1 and 1/4.
To express percentage increase as a multiplier, use fractions greater than 1.
Ensure denominators are reduced to lowest terms.

callouts.p: Treat percentages over 100% by putting the percentage value over 100 and simplifying.

core.p: In applied contexts, identifying which quantity is the 'fraction' and which is the 'of' determines your fraction structure.
bullets: Read carefully for keywords: 'What fraction of [Quantity B] is [Quantity A]?'
Quantity A goes in the numerator; Quantity B goes in the denominator.
Check whether the final answer requires simplification or a mixed number.

callouts.p: The quantity following the word 'of' is always the denominator.

core.p: Higher tier questions sometimes ask you to express one rate component as a fraction of another compound rate.
bullets: Compare numerical values extracted from speed, density, or pressure formulas.
Ensure dimensional consistency before forming the ratio fraction.
Simplify resulting numerical fractions fully.

callouts.p: Do not mix units like km/h with m/s without converting them first.

core.p: Grade 9 questions may ask you to prove statements about fractions greater than 1 using algebraic substitution and manipulation.
bullets: Set up general expressions representing integers or sequential variables.
Form the fraction and simplify algebraically.
Interpret the resulting algebraic fraction to prove whether it is always greater than 1.

callouts.p: A fraction where numerator, denominator, or both contain algebraic expressions.

core.p: Always check your fraction by converting it to a decimal or percentage to test if it aligns with the contextual reality of the problem.
bullets: If a question asks for A as a fraction of B, and A > B, your fraction must be greater than 1.
Use your calculator to verify fraction simplification in Component 2.
Ensure working out clearly shows the initial fraction before simplification marks are awarded.

callouts.p: If the part is larger than the whole, your fraction must be top-heavy (>1). If it's smaller, it must be proper (<1).

analogy.t: The Pizza Parlour and Extra Slices
analogy.p: Imagine standard pizzas cut into 8 slices each. If you eat 5 slices, you have 5/8 of a pizza (less than 1, a proper fraction). But if you and your friends eat 11 slices in total, you have consumed 11/8 of a pizza (greater than 1, an improper fraction). The reference whole (8 slices in one pizza) always stays on the bottom as your denominator, while the total number of slices eaten goes on top. The analogy breaks down when dealing with algebraic quantities or abstract units like kilograms and grams, where physical slices cannot represent negative or variable quantities.

terms.d: A fraction where the numerator is strictly less than the denominator, representing a value between 0 and 1.
A fraction where the numerator is greater than or equal to the denominator, representing a value of 1 or more.
A number consisting of an integer and a proper fraction combined.
The top number in a fraction representing the part being considered.
The bottom number in a fraction representing the reference whole or total.
The largest positive integer that divides evenly into two or more numbers, used to simplify fractions.
A comparison of a specific subgroup to the entire collection of items.
A comparison between two distinct subgroups within a total population.
A fraction containing algebraic terms in the numerator, denominator, or both.
The requirement that all quantities in a comparison share the exact same unit of measurement.
A percentage representation that corresponds directly to a fraction greater than 1.
The process of reducing a fraction to its lowest terms by cancelling common factors.

mistakes.w: Putting the reference quantity (the 'of' part) on the numerator
mistakes.r: The reference quantity must always be the denominator.

mistakes.w: Comparing quantities with mixed units (e.g., 50 cm and 2 m as 50/2)
mistakes.r: Convert both quantities to the same unit before forming the fraction (50 / 200).

mistakes.w: Panicking when the numerator is larger than the denominator and writing it upside down
mistakes.r: Fractions greater than 1 are completely valid and expected on Higher Tier papers.

mistakes.w: Failing to simplify fractions fully to their lowest terms
mistakes.r: Always divide numerator and denominator by their HCF.

mistakes.w: Writing time as a decimal instead of converting to minutes (e.g., 30 mins as 0.3 hours)
mistakes.r: Convert time into a common unit (minutes) or express as fractional hours (30/60 = 1/2).

mistakes.w: Cancelling terms incorrectly in algebraic fractions (e.g., cancelling across addition signs)
mistakes.r: Factorise fully before cancelling common factors.

mistakes.w: Confusing part-to-part with part-to-whole when given a ratio
mistakes.r: Sum the ratio parts to find the total denominator for part-to-whole fractions.

exam.q: Express 35 cm as a fraction of 2 metres. Give your fraction in its simplest form.
exam.tip: Always convert units first before attempting simplification.

exam.q: Express 75 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours. Give your answer as a fraction greater than 1 in its simplest form.
exam.tip: Read the question carefully; even though it mentions 'greater than 1', if the part is smaller than the whole the fraction will be proper.

exam.q: Container A holds 4.5 litres of water. Container B holds 3 litres of water. Express the volume of Container A as a fraction of the volume of Container B.
exam.tip: Improper fractions like 3/2 are fully accepted.

exam.q: In a school, the ratio of boys to girls is 4 : 5. Express the number of boys as a fraction of the total number of students.
exam.tip: Remember total parts form the denominator for part-to-whole fractions.

exam.q: Simplify algebraically: express 6x^2 y as a fraction of 9xy^2.
exam.tip: Cancel numerical coefficients and powers of variables separately.

exam.q: A bag contains red, blue, and green counters in the ratio 2 : 3 : 5. Express the number of green counters as a fraction of the number of red counters.
exam.tip: Check if it asks for part-to-part or part-to-whole. This is part-to-part.

exam.q: Express 140% as a fraction in its simplest form.
exam.tip: Percentages over 100% always result in fractions greater than 1.

exam.q: Object X has a mass of 450 grams. Object Y has a mass of 0.3 kilograms. Express the mass of Object X as a fraction of the mass of Object Y.
exam.tip: Convert kg to g by multiplying by 1000.

exam.q: Ali spends £18 out of his monthly savings of £12. Express the amount spent as a fraction of his savings.
exam.tip: Do not assume the smaller number must go on top.

exam.q: Express the algebraic expression (x^2 - 9) as a fraction of (2x + 6) in its simplest form.
exam.tip: Always factorise quadratic and linear expressions before cancelling.

worked.q: Express 48 minutes as a fraction of 3 hours. Give your answer in its simplest form.
steps: Step 1: Convert 3 hours into minutes. 3 * 60 = 180 minutes.
Step 2: Form the fraction with the part on top and the whole on the bottom: 48 / 180.
Step 3: Find the Highest Common Factor of 48 and 180, which is 12.
Step 4: Divide numerator and denominator by 12: (48 / 12) / (180 / 12) = 4 / 15.

worked.q: A container holds 2.4 kg of flour. A baker uses 3.6 kg of flour. Express the amount used as a fraction of the amount originally in the container.
steps: Step 1: Verify units. Both are in kilograms, so no conversion is needed.
Step 2: Identify the part used (3.6 kg) and the whole original amount (2.4 kg).
Step 3: Form the fraction: 3.6 / 2.4.
Step 4: Multiply numerator and denominator by 10 to remove decimals: 36 / 24.
Step 5: Simplify by dividing by HCF 12: 3 / 2 (or 1.5).

maths_eduqas_h.2.5.summary: Mastering the division of quantities into given ratios and applying them to real-world contexts such as currency conversion, map scaling, and ingredient mixing is vital for achieving a grade 9 in Eduqas GCSE Mathematics. This guide covers methodically structuring ratio problems using total parts, setting up algebraic ratios, solving multi-step scaling challenges, and avoiding common traps in both calculator and non-calculator papers.

core.h: 1. Fundamental Principles of Dividing Quantities into a Ratio
core.p: Dividing a quantity into a given ratio means partitioning a total amount into proportional shares. To solve these problems successfully, you must always begin by finding the total number of parts, then divide the overall quantity by this total to find the value of a single part, and finally multiply that single part value by each component of the given ratio.
bullets: Add all the numbers in the ratio together to find the total number of parts.
Divide the total quantity given in the question by the total number of parts to find the value of 1 part.
Multiply the value of 1 part by each individual number in the ratio to find the final share amounts.
Always check your final answers by adding them back together; their sum must equal the original total quantity.

callouts.p: The sum of your divided shares must always equal the original quantity. If it does not, recalculate your value of 1 part.
Write down what each number in the ratio represents before starting calculations to avoid mixing up shares.

core.h: 2. Algebraic Ratio Sharing and Multi-Step Problems
core.p: At higher tier, ratios are frequently linked through unknown algebraic variables or multi-step connections where quantities are shared unevenly or changed subsequently. You must use algebra to represent unknown multipliers and set up linear equations based on the relationships stated in the question.
bullets: Represent unknown quantities using an algebraic multiplier, such as 3x and 5x for a ratio of 3:5.
Form equations when given differences between shares, such as 'Person A gets 24 more than Person B'.
Solve for x carefully, ensuring you substitute x back into all parts of the ratio to find the required final values.
Be prepared for questions where parts of the ratio are added to or removed after the initial division.

callouts.p: A variable used to represent the common scaling factor shared across all parts of a ratio.
When a question states one share is greater than another by a value, equate the difference between their ratio parts to that value, not the total.

fig.cap: Visualising a ratio division of 60 into parts of 2, 3, and 5, showing 10 units per part.

core.h: 3. Real Contexts: Currency Conversion and Exchange Rates
core.p: Exchange rates establish a direct ratio between two different currencies. Applying ratio principles allows you to convert money accurately from one currency to another using multiplication or division based on whether you are scaling up or down.
bullets: Identify the given exchange rate ratio, such as £1 : $1.25 or 1 EUR : 0.85 GBP.
Set up a proportion table or multiplier equation to convert foreign currency to home currency and vice versa.
Multiply by the exchange rate when converting from the base currency to the foreign currency.
Divide by the exchange rate when converting from the foreign currency back to the base currency.

callouts.p: Always check which currency is worth 1 unit in the given ratio before performing your multiplication or division.
If the exchange rate is £1 = $1.30, your US dollar amount should always be numerically larger than your British pound amount.

core.h: 4. Real Contexts: Scaling Recipes and Ingredients
core.p: Recipe scaling requires maintaining a strict ratio between different ingredients to preserve taste, texture, and consistency when making larger or smaller quantities. Every ingredient must be multiplied by the exact same scaling factor.
bullets: Find the scaling factor by dividing the target number of servings by the original number of servings.
Multiply every single ingredient quantity in the original recipe by this exact scaling factor.
Be careful with units when scaling; convert grams to kilograms or millilitres to litres if required before or after calculation.
For inverse mixing problems, determine the limiting ingredient when stocks of specific items are constrained.

callouts.p: The multiplier by which all parts of a recipe or geometric shape are uniformly increased or decreased.
Never add a fixed amount to ingredients when scaling up a recipe; ratios require multiplicative scaling, not additive scaling.

fig.cap: Scaling a recipe from 4 servings to 10 servings using a multiplier of 2.5.

core.p: Mixing problems involve combining two or more solutions, alloys, or mixtures with different component ratios to create a new combined ratio or concentration. Success depends on breaking each mixture down into its absolute fractional parts before combining them.
bullets: Express each component of a mixture as a fraction of the total volume or mass (e.g., 3 parts gold to 2 parts copper is 3/5 gold).
When mixing two containers, calculate the exact amount of each pure substance in both containers separately.
Add the total masses or volumes of each pure substance together to form the new combined ratio.
Simplify the final combined ratio fully by finding the highest common factor.

callouts.p: Always convert ratios into fractions when combining mixtures to correctly account for differing total batch sizes.
Draw a clear table with columns for Ingredient 1, Ingredient 2, and Total to keep track of combined values.

core.h: 6. Combining Two Ratios into a Three-Part Ratio
core.p: A common higher-tier exam technique requires you to combine two separate ratios, such as A:B and B:C, into a single unified ratio A:B:C. This is achieved by finding the lowest common multiple of the shared term.
bullets: Identify the common letter that appears in both given ratios (for example, B is in both A:B and B:C).
Find the lowest common multiple (LCM) of the two numbers representing that shared letter in the respective ratios.
Scale both ratios up so that the shared letter has the exact same numerical value in both.
Combine the scaled ratios into a single three-part ratio in the form A:B:C and simplify if possible.

callouts.p: The lowest common multiple used to align the numerical value of a common entity across two separate ratios.
Never write A:B = 2:3 and B:C = 4:5 as A:B:C = 2:3:5. You must align the B term first.

core.h: 7. Ratio and Fractions Interconversion in Context
core.p: Ratio statements and fraction statements are interchangeable ways of describing proportional relationships. Knowing how to convert fluidly between them is vital when solving advanced multi-step real-world problems.
bullets: If a quantity is divided in the ratio a:b, the first share is fraction a/(a+b) of the total, and the second share is b/(a+b).
To convert a fraction a/b into a ratio, write it as a: (b - a) if comparing parts of a whole, or a:b if comparing part to whole.
Use fractional multipliers in word problems when a direct share amount is requested rather than the full set of parts.
Check whether a question asks for a 'part-to-part' ratio or a 'part-to-whole' fraction.

callouts.p: A ratio like 3:4 compares two parts. The fraction 3/7 compares part 3 to the total whole of 7.
Converting ratios to fractions makes calculating percentage increases or decreases on specific shares much faster.

core.p: Map scales are expressed as ratios representing the relationship between distance on a map and the corresponding actual distance on the ground. Both units must be converted into the same metric before writing or applying the ratio.
bullets: A map ratio of 1 : 50,000 means 1 cm on the map represents 50,000 cm in real life.
Always convert ground centimetres into metres (divide by 100) or kilometres (divide by 100,000) for practical interpretation.
To find real distance, multiply map distance by the scale factor.
To find map distance, divide real distance by the scale factor.

callouts.p: A map scale written as a dimensionless ratio such as 1:25000 where units are identical on both sides.
Forgetting to convert centimeters to kilometers (dividing by 100,000 instead of 1,000) is a frequent error.

core.h: 9. Ratio in Geometric Similarity and Length Scaling
core.p: When figures are similar, all corresponding linear dimensions are in the same ratio. While areas scale by the square of the ratio and volumes scale by the cube, the fundamental ratio between any two matching lengths remains linear.
bullets: Similar shapes have corresponding side lengths in a constant ratio k.
If the ratio of linear dimensions is a:b, the ratio of their areas is a^2 : b^2.
If the ratio of linear dimensions is a:b, the ratio of their volumes is a^3 : b^3.
Use linear ratios to find unknown side lengths of similar triangles or polygons embedded in complex diagrams.

callouts.p: Area scales with the square of the linear scale factor. Do not multiply linear ratios directly for area problems.
Look for parallel lines in geometric diagrams to immediately establish equal angles and similar triangle ratios.

core.h: 10. Best Buys and Unit Pricing Ratios
core.p: Unit pricing involves comparing value for money by establishing a ratio or rate per single unit of mass, volume, or count. This is a standard applied ratio context in non-calculator and calculator papers alike.
bullets: Calculate the unit cost by dividing the total price by the quantity (e.g., Price per 100g or Price per 1 litre).
Ensure both items being compared are converted to identical units before calculating unit cost.
The best buy is always the option with the lowest cost per single unit.
Be careful when packaging sizes differ significantly; check whether bulk buying genuinely reduces unit price.

callouts.p: The cost of a single unit of weight, volume, or quantity used to compare value between different products.
Always standardise items to the exact same unit size (e.g., per 100g) before making your comparison conclusion.

core.h: 11. Proportion Graphs and Direct Ratio Lines
core.p: Direct proportion relationships form straight lines passing through the origin on a Cartesian plane. The gradient of this line represents the constant ratio or rate of change between the two variables.
bullets: An equation representing direct proportion is written in the form y = kx, where k is the constant of proportionality.
The graph of direct proportion is always a straight line passing through the coordinates (0,0).
The gradient of the line equals the ratio y/x at any given point on the line.
Use coordinates from a given point on the proportion line to calculate the exact value of the constant k.

callouts.p: The constant multiplier k that relates two directly proportional variables in the equation y = kx.
If a straight line does not pass through the origin (0,0), the variables are in linear correlation, not direct proportion.

core.p: Top-grade exam questions frequently combine ratio sharing with percentages, algebra, or simultaneous equations. Approaching these systematically by defining variables clearly and writing down intermediate steps ensures maximum marks.
bullets: Translate wordy problem statements into algebraic ratio equations step by step.
Substitute known values into ratios to establish simultaneous equations if two independent ratios are provided.
Always write out your final answer clearly with appropriate units.
Review your working out to ensure no intermediate rounding errors occurred before the final step.

callouts.p: In complex multi-variable questions, express all variables in terms of a single letter before solving.
Method marks are awarded readily in Eduqas papers; write down every ratio addition and division clearly.

analogy.t: The Artist's Palette and Paint Mixing
analogy.p: Imagine mixing paint to get a specific shade of green using a ratio of 2 parts blue to 3 parts yellow. The total mix is 5 parts. If you need a larger batch for a massive canvas, you don't just add 2 tubes of blue and 3 tubes of yellow (additive thinking); you multiply every colour tube by the exact same scaling factor to maintain the exact same hue. This mirrors mathematical ratio scaling where all components must scale in lockstep. However, the analogy breaks down if chemical reactions occur when mixing real paint that alter opacity or saturation non-linearly, whereas mathematical ratios remain perfectly constant.

terms.d: A mathematical comparison of two or more quantities showing the relative sizes of those values.
The sum of all individual numbers in a given ratio used to partition a total quantity.
The fundamental quantity obtained by dividing the total amount by the total number of ratio parts.
The ratio at which one currency can be exchanged for another.
The multiplier applied to all parts of a ratio, recipe, or geometric shape to increase or decrease its size.
A map scale written as a ratio where map units and ground units are expressed in the same measurement units.
The multiplier k in a direct proportion relationship y = kx.
A ratio comparing one subset of a whole directly to another subset of the same whole.
A comparison expressing a single share as a fraction of the entire total quantity.
The smallest positive integer that is a multiple of two or more numbers, used for combining ratios.
The monetary cost per single unit of measure, mass, or volume.
Geometric figures that have the same shape with corresponding side lengths in a constant ratio.

mistakes.w: Adding the ratio numbers to the final quantities instead of multiplying by the value of 1 part.
mistakes.r: Find the total parts, divide the total quantity to find 1 part, then multiply each ratio number by that 1 part value.

mistakes.w: Writing A:B:C = 2:3:5 when given A:B = 2:3 and B:C = 3:5.
mistakes.r: Verify that the shared term B has the same numerical value in both ratios before combining them into a three-part ratio.

mistakes.w: Using additive scaling when increasing a recipe or mixture quantity (e.g. adding 5 to all ingredients).
mistakes.r: Always use multiplicative scaling; multiply every ingredient quantity by the identical scaling factor.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to convert units when working with map scales or metric ratios (e.g. keeping cm and km mixed).
mistakes.r: Convert all measurements into identical units (usually centimetres or metres) before establishing the scale ratio.

mistakes.w: Inverting exchange rate divisions, multiplying when you should divide.
mistakes.r: Check the currency base unit: multiply to convert home to foreign currency, divide to convert foreign back to home.

mistakes.w: Treating area ratios as identical to linear length ratios in similar shapes.
mistakes.r: Square the linear scale factor to find the area scale factor, and cube it to find the volume scale factor.

mistakes.w: Assuming a straight line on a graph represents direct proportion even if it does not pass through the origin.
mistakes.r: A direct proportion graph must be a straight line passing strictly through the origin coordinate (0,0).

exam.q: A sum of £450 is divided between Ben and Chloe in the ratio 2 : 7. Work out how much Chloe receives.
exam.tip: Always state the total number of parts clearly before calculating the value of 1 part.

exam.q: The ratio of boys to girls in a club is 4 : 5. There are 72 children in total in the club. How many more girls are there than boys?
model: Difference in parts = 5 - 4 = 1 part, so 1 * 8 = 8 more girls
exam.tip: You can find individual totals first (32 boys, 40 girls) and subtract, but finding the difference in parts is faster.

exam.q: A recipe for 6 pancakes requires 150g of flour and 2 eggs. Find the amount of flour needed to make 15 pancakes.
exam.tip: Find the decimal or fractional scaling factor by dividing target servings by original servings.

exam.q: Given that A : B = 3 : 4 and B : C = 8 : 15, find the ratio A : B : C in its simplest form.
model: Scale A : B by multiplying by 2 so B becomes 8 -> A : B = 6 : 8
Combine with B : C = 8 : 15 to get 6 : 8 : 15
Check if simplest form (HCF of 6, 8, 15 is 1), so final ratio is 6 : 8 : 15
exam.tip: Align the shared letter by finding the lowest common multiple of its two values.

exam.q: A bag contains red counters and blue counters in the ratio 3 : 5. 16 more blue counters are added, and the ratio becomes 1 : 2. How many red counters are in the bag?
model: Let red counters be 3x and blue counters be 5x
exam.tip: Set up an algebraic fraction representing the ratio change and cross-multiply to solve for x.

exam.q: An alloy is made by mixing metal X and metal Y in the ratio 5 : 2 by mass. Metal X has a density of 8 g/cm^3 and metal Y has a density of 10 g/cm^3. Find the density of the alloy.
model: Let mass of X be 5g and Y be 2g (total mass = 7g)
Volume of X = 5 / 8 cm^3; Volume of Y = 2 / 10 = 1/5 cm^3
Density of alloy = Total Mass / Total Volume = 7 / (33/40) = 280 / 33 = 8.48 g/cm^3
exam.tip: Assign convenient masses proportional to the ratio numbers to simplify density calculations.

exam.q: Two similar containers have heights in the ratio 2 : 5. The volume of the smaller container is 50 cm^3. Find the volume of the larger container.
exam.tip: Cube the linear scale factor when working with volumes of similar objects.

exam.q: The exchange rate is £1 = $1.28 and €1 = £0.85. Convert $500 into Euros, giving your answer to the nearest cent.
exam.tip: Always perform intermediate currency steps with full calculator precision and round only at the final answer.

exam.q: Share £108 in the ratio 3 : 4 : 2.
exam.tip: Check your answer: 36 + 48 + 24 = 108.

worked.q: A sum of money is shared between Ali, Beth, and Carl in the ratio 4 : 5 : 6. Ali receives £36 less than Carl. Work out the total sum of money shared.
steps: Identify the ratio parts for Ali and Carl: Ali is 4 parts and Carl is 6 parts.
Find the difference in parts between Carl and Ali: 6 parts - 4 parts = 2 parts.
Equate this difference in parts to the given money difference: 2 parts = £36.
Calculate the value of 1 part: £36 / 2 = £18.
Find the total number of parts in the entire ratio: 4 + 5 + 6 = 15 parts.
Multiply the total parts by the value of 1 part to find the total sum: 15 * £18 = £270.

worked.q: Container A and Container B hold acid and water mixed in the ratios 1 : 3 and 3 : 5 respectively. Equal volumes of Container A and Container B are mixed together. Find the ratio of acid to water in the final mixture.
steps: Find total parts for Container A: 1 + 3 = 4 parts. Acid fraction = 1/4, Water fraction = 3/4.
Find total parts for Container B: 3 + 5 = 8 parts. Acid fraction = 3/8, Water fraction = 5/8.
To make volumes equal, scale Container A's fractions by multiplying by 2 so its total parts equal 8: Acid = 2/8, Water = 6/8.
Add the acid fractions together: 2/8 + 3/8 = 5/8 acid.
Add the water fractions together: 6/8 + 5/8 = 11/8 water.
Form the final ratio of acid to water: 5/8 : 11/8, which simplifies to 5 : 11.

maths_eduqas_h.2.11.summary: Mastering compound units under the Eduqas GCSE Higher specification requires a robust understanding of formulas relating speed, rates of pay, unit pricing, density, and pressure. Grade 9 success relies on converting units consistently before calculation, manipulating algebraic formulas fluently, and interpreting compound measures as rates of change in complex multi-step problems.

core.p: Compound units are formed by multiplying or dividing two or more base units to describe a rate of change or a physical property. In exams, you must ensure all quantities are converted into consistent base units before substituting them into formulas.
bullets: Formed from algebraic combinations of fundamental units such as metres, kilograms, and seconds.
Dimensional analysis can check if a formula is correct by verifying unit consistency.
Always check prefixes and standard conversions (e.g., cm to m, grams to kg, minutes to hours).

callouts.p: A unit of measurement derived from a combination of base SI units through multiplication or division.
Write out the formula in symbols before substituting any numbers to secure method marks.

core.p: Speed is the rate of change of distance with respect to time. The foundational relationship is Speed equals Distance divided by Time. In higher-tier questions, you must handle recurring decimals in time, convert between km/h and m/s, and interpret distance-time graphs.
bullets: Formula: Speed = Distance / Time (S = D / T).
Alternative arrangements: Distance = Speed x Time, Time = Distance / Speed.
To convert km/h to m/s, divide by 3.6. To convert m/s to km/h, multiply by 3.6.
Beware of time notation: 0.5 hours is 30 minutes, not 50 minutes.

callouts.p: 4 hours 15 minutes is 4.25 hours, NOT 4.15 hours. Always convert minutes to a fraction or decimal of an hour by dividing by 60.

core.h: Rates of Pay and Unit Pricing
core.p: Rates of pay calculate earnings over a specified time period, whilst unit pricing determines the cost per individual unit of mass, volume, or count to compare value for money. These concepts test proportional reasoning and decimal arithmetic in non-calculator papers.
bullets: Rate of pay: Total Pay = Hourly Rate x Number of Hours Worked.
Overtime rates: Usually a multiplier applied to the standard hourly rate (e.g., time-and-a-half is 1.5x).
Unit pricing: Cost per Unit = Total Price / Total Quantity.
Always compare items using the same base unit (e.g., price per 100g or price per 1kg).

callouts.p: When asked for best value, always calculate the cost per single unit unless specified otherwise.

core.p: Density measures how tightly packed matter is within a given space. It is defined as mass per unit volume. In higher tier questions, you may need to find volumes of composite shapes like cylinders, cones, or spheres before calculating density or mass.
bullets: Formula: Density = Mass / Volume (rho = m / V).
Common units: g/cm^3 or kg/m^3.
Conversion rule: 1 g/cm^3 = 1000 kg/m^3.
Mass = Density x Volume; Volume = Mass / Density.

callouts.p: The mass of a substance per unit volume, expressed in units such as kg/m^3 or g/cm^3.

core.p: Pressure is defined as the force applied perpendicular to the surface per unit area over which that force is distributed. A smaller surface area subjected to the same force creates a significantly higher pressure.
bullets: Formula: Pressure = Force / Area (P = F / A).
Units: Pascals (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N/m^2, or N/cm^2.
Force = Pressure x Area; Area = Force / Pressure.
Ensure force is in Newtons (N) and area is in square metres (m^2) for standard Pascal calculations.

callouts.p: If length is converted by multiplying by 100 (cm to m), area must be multiplied by 100^2 = 10,000. Be extremely careful with squared unit conversions.

core.p: At Grade 9, compound unit questions frequently feature algebraic expressions rather than fixed numerical values. You must set up equations using formulas like Speed = Distance / Time and solve for unknown variables.
bullets: Express unknown distances, times, or speeds using algebra (e.g., let time be t).
Formulate algebraic fractions for compound quantities.
Solve resulting linear or quadratic equations accurately.
Check domain restrictions (e.g., time or speed cannot be negative).

callouts.p: Define your variables clearly at the start of the solution (e.g., 'Let the speed of the car be x').

core.p: Examination questions often combine multiple compound units, such as calculating the mass of an object from its density and volume, then determining the pressure it exerts on a surface.
bullets: Break the problem down into sequential logical steps.
Find intermediate values first (e.g., calculate volume, then mass).
Carry exact values through calculations; do not round prematurely until the final answer.
Check that final units match what the question demands.

callouts.p: Keep at least 4 significant figures in intermediate steps during calculator papers to avoid rounding errors.

core.p: Average speed is calculated over an entire journey by dividing total distance by total time. It does not account for stationary periods or changes in speed during the journey, whereas instantaneous speed is the speed at a specific moment.
bullets: Average Speed = Total Distance / Total Time.
Common error: Finding the mean of two speeds instead of using total distance over total time.
On a distance-time graph, average speed is the gradient of the chord connecting start and end points.

callouts.p: If a person travels 10 miles at 20 mph and 10 miles at 60 mph, their average speed is NOT 40 mph. Total distance is 20, total time is 0.5 + 0.166 = 0.666 hours, giving an average speed of 30 mph.

core.p: Exam questions deliberately mismatch units to test vigilance. You must convert dimensions into a uniform system before applying compound unit formulas.
bullets: Length conversions: 1 m = 100 cm = 1000 mm.
Mass conversions: 1 kg = 1000 g.
Volume conversions: 1 m^3 = 1,000,000 cm^3.
Time conversions: 1 hour = 60 minutes = 3600 seconds.

callouts.p: Because 1 m = 100 cm, cubing both sides gives (1 m)^3 = (100 cm)^3, meaning 1 m^3 = 1,000,000 cm^3.

core.p: Rates of flow measure volume passing a point per unit time (e.g., litres per minute), while consumption measures resource usage per unit distance or time (e.g., fuel economy in miles per gallon).
bullets: Flow Rate = Volume / Time.
Fuel Economy = Distance Travelled / Fuel Consumed.
Use proportional reasoning to scale flow rates for longer or shorter durations.
Pay close attention to imperial and metric conversions if specified in the exam context.

callouts.p: If a pipe fills a tank faster (higher flow rate), the time taken is inversely proportional.

analogy.p: Think of compound units like baking a recipe where ingredients must maintain a strict ratio to yield the right taste. If you double the flour, you must double the liquid to keep the density of the dough identical. Where this analogy breaks down is that physical compound measures like pressure involve nonlinear spatial interactions (area squared), whereas baking ratios scale linearly.

terms.d: A unit of measurement constructed by multiplying or dividing fundamental base units.
The rate of change of distance, calculated as distance divided by time.
Mass per unit volume of a substance, expressed in units like kg/m^3.
Force applied per unit perpendicular area, measured in Pascals.
The SI unit of pressure, equivalent to one Newton per square metre.
Total distance travelled divided by total time taken for the journey.
The volume of fluid passing through a system per unit of time.
The cost of a commodity expressed per single standard unit of weight or volume.
Money earned per unit of time worked.
The checking of mathematical relations for consistency of units.
A measure of the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms.
The amount of three-dimensional space occupied by an object.

mistakes.w: Averaging two speeds to find average speed (e.g., (40 + 60) / 2 = 50).
mistakes.r: Calculate total distance divided by total time.

mistakes.w: Converting 4 hours 30 minutes to 4.3 hours.
mistakes.r: Convert minutes to a decimal fraction by dividing by 60 (4.5 hours).

mistakes.w: Converting cm^2 to m^2 by dividing by 100.
mistakes.r: Divide by 10,000 (100^2) because area scales quadratically.

mistakes.w: Multiplying density by volume when asked for volume.
mistakes.r: Rearrange formula: Volume = Mass / Density.

mistakes.w: Using grams and kilograms in the same density calculation without converting.
mistakes.r: Ensure all units are homogenous before substituting into formulas.

mistakes.w: Treating force and pressure as interchangeable terms.
mistakes.r: Force is a push or pull; pressure is force distributed over a specific area.

mistakes.w: Rounding intermediate calculator values to 1 decimal place.
mistakes.r: Keep full calculator display and round only the final answer.

exam.q: A car travels 180 miles in 2 hours 30 minutes. Calculate the average speed of the car in miles per hour.
exam.tip: Always convert minutes to decimal hours before dividing.

exam.q: A solid metal cylinder has a mass of 500g and a volume of 50cm^3. Calculate the density of the cylinder in g/cm^3.
exam.tip: Check that mass and volume units match the required output units.

exam.q: Box A contains 400g of cereal for 2.40 pounds. Box B contains 750g of cereal for 4.20 pounds. Determine which box offers better value for money.
model: Calculate unit price for Box A: 240p / 400 = 0.6p per gram
Calculate unit price for Box B: 420p / 750 = 0.56p per gram
Conclusion: Box B is better value with supporting working
exam.tip: Find the cost per 100g or cost per 1g clearly for both items.

exam.q: A block exerts a force of 120 Newtons on a surface. The area of contact is 0.4 m^2. Calculate the pressure exerted in Pascals.
exam.tip: 1 Pascal equals 1 N/m^2.

exam.q: A runner completes a 10 km race in 40 minutes. Calculate their average speed in metres per second.
model: Convert time to seconds: 40 x 60 = 2400 s
exam.tip: Perform conversions for distance and time separately before dividing.

exam.q: A liquid has a density of 0.8 g/cm^3. Work out the mass of 2.5 litres of this liquid in kilograms.
model: Convert litres to cm^3: 2.5 litres = 2500 cm^3
Calculate mass in grams: 0.8 x 2500 = 2000 g
exam.tip: Remember 1 litre = 1000 cm^3.

exam.q: The pressure of a gas is 50 kPa and it acts over an area of 200 cm^2. Calculate the force exerted in Newtons.
model: Rearrange formula: Force = Pressure x Area
exam.tip: Be extremely careful when converting cm^2 to m^2.

exam.q: A train travels at 80 km/h for 45 minutes, then at 120 km/h for 1 hour 30 minutes. Calculate the total distance travelled.
exam.tip: Break journey into distinct legs and calculate distance for each.

exam.q: An object has a volume of 3 m^3 and a density of 2.5 g/cm^3. Calculate its mass in kilograms.
model: Convert density to kg/m^3: 2.5 x 1000 = 2500 kg/m^3
State formula: Mass = Density x Volume
exam.tip: Converting density units first makes volume multiplication straightforward.

exam.q: A worker earns 12.50 pounds per hour for a 35-hour week. Overtime is paid at 1.5 times the standard rate. If they work 42 hours in a week, calculate their total weekly pay.
exam.tip: Calculate standard pay and overtime pay separately before adding.

worked.q: A solid gold sphere has a radius of 5 cm. The density of gold is 19.3 g/cm^3. Given that the volume of a sphere is V = (4/3) pi r^3, calculate the mass of the sphere in kilograms, giving your answer to 3 significant figures.
steps: Calculate the volume of the sphere using V = (4/3) pi (5)^3 = (500/3) pi cm^3 approx 523.60 cm^3.
Calculate the mass in grams by multiplying volume by density: m = 523.60 x 19.3 approx 10,105.48 g.
Convert mass to kilograms by dividing by 1000: 10.105 kg.
Round to 3 significant figures: 10.1 kg.

worked.q: A container holds 450 litres of water. It is leaking at a constant rate of 15 cm^3 per second. How many hours will it take for the container to empty completely? (1 litre = 1000 cm^3)
steps: Convert total volume to cm^3: 450 litres = 450,000 cm^3.
Calculate total seconds required: 450,000 / 15 = 30,000 seconds.
Convert seconds to hours by dividing by 3600 (since 1 hour = 3600 seconds): 30,000 / 3600 = 8.333... hours.

maths_eduqas_h.2.9.summary: Mastering percentages for Eduqas GCSE Higher requires moving beyond primary school methods to use single multiplier values, backwards reverse percentage calculations, and correct simple interest setups. You must handle percentages significantly above 100% for profit markups, price increases, and growth models without falling into common arithmetic traps. This comprehensive guide connects percentage change formulas, original value recovery, and standard simple interest models directly to top-band exam requirements.

core.p: A percentage is simply a fraction out of 100. In higher-tier Eduqas papers, treating percentages as decimal multipliers is vital for speed and algebraic setup. A multiplier is the single decimal or fraction you multiply an amount by to scale it directly.
bullets: Convert any percentage to a decimal by dividing by 100.
Increase by p% means multiplying by (1 + p/100).
Decrease by p% means multiplying by (1 - p/100).
Percentages over 100% involve multipliers greater than 1.0.

callouts.p: The decimal factor used to scale a quantity up or down in a single multiplication step.
For non-calculator papers, keep multipliers as fractions or use 10% and 1% building blocks.

core.p: To calculate the percentage change between an original value and a new value, compare the absolute difference to the original amount. The denominator is always the starting original value, never the new value.
bullets: Step 1: Find the actual difference (New - Old or Old - New).
Step 2: Divide the difference by the original value.
Step 3: Multiply the result by 100 to convert to a percentage.
Formula: Percentage Change = (Actual Difference / Original Value) * 100.

callouts.p: Dividing the difference by the new value instead of the original value is the most common exam error.

fig.cap: Visual breakdown of the percentage change calculation steps for GCSE Higher tier.

Percentage Change = Fraction * 100</text></svg>

core.p: When a percentage increase or decrease has already been applied and you need to find the starting value before the change, do not work backwards by reversing the operation. Instead, form an equation using a multiplier.
bullets: Let the unknown original value be x.
Set up the equation: x * multiplier = given final value.
Solve by dividing the final value by the multiplier.
Never add or subtract the percentage off the final value.

callouts.p: Original Value = Final Value / Multiplier. Never subtract the percentage from the final total.

core.p: Higher tier Eduqas exams regularly test percentages greater than 100%. These represent situations where a quantity more than doubles, triples, or grows beyond its initial baseline.
bullets: An increase of 150% means the new value is 100% + 150% = 250% of the original.
The multiplier for a 150% increase is 2.50.
If an item is sold at 320% of its cost price, the markup percentage is 220%.
Algebraically manipulate expressions involving percentages over 100% with care.

callouts.p: Do not use 1.50 as the multiplier for a 150% increase; 1.50 represents a 50% increase. A 150% increase uses 2.50.

core.p: Simple interest calculates a fixed percentage of the initial principal amount for every time period specified. The interest earned each year is constant because it does not compound onto previous interest.
bullets: Formula: I = (P * r * t) / 100, where P is principal, r is annual rate, t is time in years.
Total amount = Principal + Total Interest earned.
Linear growth: plotted on a straight line graph over time.
Used primarily in specific financial instruments and basic borrowing.

callouts.p: Interest calculated solely on the initial principal sum, remaining constant across every time period.
